options.label: A
options.latex: In some connected networks, there may be more than one minimum spanning tree.

options.label: B
options.latex: In some connected networks, there may be more than one shortest path between two of the vertices.

options.label: C
options.latex: In all connected networks, the shortest path between two vertices will be located on a minimum spanning tree of the network.

options.label: D
options.latex: In all connected networks, the sum of the degrees of the vertices is double the number of edges.

parts.latex: For connected networks, which of the following is NOT true?

solutions.latex:
Option A is true: a network with equal edge weights can have several minimum spanning trees.

Option B is true: two different routes can have the same shortest length.

Option D is true: the sum of the degrees is twice the number of edges.

Option C is not true: a shortest path between two vertices need not use only edges of the minimum spanning tree, since the tree minimises total length, not individual path lengths.

So the statement that is NOT true is option C.

A spanning tree connects all vertices using no cycles, with one fewer edge than the number of vertices.

Option C is the graph that includes every vertex of the network and contains no cycle, so it is a spanning tree.

This is option C.

The diagram shows the cost of direct flights, in dollars, between eight cities in Asia, as offered by Asia Insight Airlines.

\exfigure{722_q13_1}

eight city vertices for drawing the minimum spanning tree

parts.latex: How many edges on the network diagram would form a minimum spanning tree?

Asia Insight Airlines offers two direct flights from the city of Thimphu, Bhutan:

Thimphu to Seoul for \$630 and Thimphu to Dili for \$350.

What is the length of the minimum spanning tree that includes Thimphu?

solutions.latex:
A spanning tree on $n$ vertices has $n-1$ edges. There are $8$ cities.
$$\begin{aligned} n-1 &= 8-1 \\ &= 7 \text{ edges} \end{aligned}$$

Choosing the cheapest edges that join all cities without forming a cycle gives the minimum spanning tree.

\exfigure{722_q13_s1}

The edges are Almaty–Chennai $330$, Almaty–Yerevan $485$, Yerevan–Bishkek $450$, Bishkek–Kabul $275$, Kabul–Dili $370$, Bishkek–Xi'an $445$, Xi'an–Seoul $620$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Length} &= 330 + 485 + 450 + 370 + 275 + 445 + 620 \\ &= 2975 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{length of minimum spanning tree} = \$2975$$
criteria: Draws a correct tree or finds the correct length, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: minimum spanning tree on the eight cities with edges Almaty–Chennai 330, Almaty–Yerevan 485, Yerevan–Bishkek 450, Bishkek–Kabul 275, Kabul–Dili 370, Bishkek–Xi'an 445, Xi'an–Seoul 620; total 2975. Rubric written by us. Source lists the edges as 7 and sum is consistent. Thimphu is not among the listed cities in the source tree, so part (c) adds the cheapest Thimphu edge 350.

solutions.latex:
Thimphu is not yet in the tree, so join it by its cheaper flight, to Dili for $\$350$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Length} &= 2975 + 350 \\ &= 3325 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{length} = \$3325$$

meta.format_note: The source's tree in (b) has 8 vertices already; adding Thimphu implies a ninth city, consistent with the source answer.

figures.cap: weighted network of roads (NOT TO SCALE)

solutions.latex:
A minimum spanning tree on 6 vertices has 5 edges. Using Kruskal's algorithm, add the shortest edges that do not form a cycle.

The edges in order are $4,\ 5,\ 5,\ 6,\ 7,\ 7,\ 8,\ 9,\ 10$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4 &&&\text{add}\\ 5 &&&\text{add}\\ 5 &&&\text{add}\\ 6 &&&\text{add}\\ 7,\ 7,\ 8 &&&\text{each would form a cycle, so reject}\\ 9 &&&\text{add (joins the top vertex)} \end{aligned}$$
The tree has edges $4,\ 5,\ 5,\ 6,\ 9$ (5 edges, total $29$).

The largest weighted edge in it is $9$, so the answer is option C.

meta.self_check: Checked with Kruskal; the top vertex connects only by 9 or 10, so 9 must be used. Verified the 5 edges connect all 6 vertices.
meta.generated_note: MCQ working written from the answer key.

5834_q3_1.notes: Weighted network: 6 vertices, 9 edges, weights placed as in the crop and clear of the edges. Left out the crop's stray scan specks on the right (rules 1, 3, 11).

solutions.latex:
A spanning tree uses every vertex of the network, is connected, and has no cycles.

The network has 7 vertices, so a spanning tree has $7-1=6$ edges.

Option A has cycles (for example the triangles at the top), so it is not a tree.

Option B leaves the central vertex isolated, so it is not connected.

Option C contains cycles (for example the triangle at the top right), so it is not a tree.

Option D joins all 7 vertices using exactly 6 edges, and it has no cycle.

$$\therefore\ \text{Option D is a spanning tree.}$$

meta.self_check: Counted vertices (7) and edges in each option; D has 6 edges, connected, acyclic.
meta.generated_note: Working written from the answer key.
